witness.desc: Lost Carolingian archetype of the entire extant Lucretian transmission (saec. VIII/IX). Written in Carolingian minuscule with 26 lines per page. Four of its leaves came loose and were attached at the end of the codex after O had been copied but before Γ was (Praef. § 3, § 11).

Codex Oblongus, Leiden, Universitaire Bibliotheken, Voss. Lat. F 30, parchment, early 9th century (reign of Charlemagne), 192 folios with 20 lines per page. The oldest, most authoritative, and complete direct witness (Praef. § 4).
First hand (scribe) of Codex Oblongus (Praef. § 5).
Dungal, Irish monk at Saint-Denis and Pavia (early 9th century); contemporary corrector of Oblongus in Anglo-Saxon script, supplying lacunae directly from the archetype Ω (Praef. § 5).
Anonymous contemporary or slightly later Carolingian correctors of Codex Oblongus (Praef. § 5).
Corrector of Codex Oblongus of the late 10th or early 11th century; glossed rare words and corrected corrupt passages with the help of another manuscript; no corrections after I 827 (Praef. § 5).

Lost Carolingian sub-archetype, twin branch to O, reconstructed through the shared consensus of Q and the fragments G, V, U. Copied from Ω after four leaves of the archetype (I 734–785, II 253–304, II 757–806, V 928–979) had fallen out and been attached at its end: hence Q and U transmit these passages after the last line of Book VI (Praef. § 3, §§ 10–11).
Codex Quadratus, Leiden, Universitaire Bibliotheken, Voss. Lat. Q 94, mid-9th century (north-eastern France), 2 columns of 28 lines (Praef. § 6).
First hand of Codex Quadratus (Praef. § 7).
Ancient Carolingian corrector of Quadratus, contemporary with the scribe (Praef. § 7, § 14).
Mid-15th-century Italian humanist corrector of Quadratus; emended through ingenious conjectures (suo Marte) without consulting additional manuscripts (Praef. § 7).
Schedae Gottorpienses, Copenhagen, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, GKS 211 2°, late 9th century; preserves I 1 – II 456 (Praef. §§ 8–9).
Schedae Vindobonenses priores, Vienna, ÖNB, Cod. Lat. 107, fols. 9–14, late 9th century; preserves II 642 – III 621 (Praef. §§ 8–9).

Schedae Vindobonenses posteriores, Vienna, ÖNB, Cod. Lat. 107, fols. 15–18, late 9th century; preserves VI 743 to end. Originally G, V, and U formed a single parchment codex copied in northern Italy (Praef. §§ 8–9).
Apographum Poggianum: the lost exemplar transcribed in Germany (1417) for Poggio Bracciolini and sent to Niccolò Niccoli in Florence in 1418 (Praef. § 17, § 20).
The corrected Poggian apograph enriched in the margins with conjectures and emendations by Poggio, Niccolò Niccoli, and their circle; consensus of direct descendants (Praef. § 20).
Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 35.30, autograph copy written by Niccolò Niccoli (Praef. § 17).
Vatican City, BAV, Reg. Lat. 1706; primary witness from III 647 onwards (first part copied from L) (Praef. § 17).
Vatican City, BAV, Patetta 312; exhibits three distinct layers of humanist correctors (Praef. § 17, § 26).
Cesena, Biblioteca Malatestiana, S 20.4 (Praef. § 17).
Oldest lost apograph derived from ξ; the branch least altered by humanistic conjectures (Praef. § 17, §§ 22–23).
Madrid, Biblioteca Nacional de España, MS 2885; most faithful extant witness of branch μ (Praef. § 17, § 23).
Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Conv. Soppr. 453 (Praef. § 17).
Consensus of manuscripts L, Aa, x and o of the ξ-family.
Lost Tuscan exemplar derived from μ before 1442 by an anonymous scholar (possibly Antonio Panormita), rich in original conjectures (Praef. § 17, §§ 24–25).
Vatican City, BAV, Vat. Lat. 3276 (copied in 1442) (Praef. § 17, § 25).
Second hand in manuscript A, added by Antonio Panormita in Naples, correcting the text to conform with α (Praef. § 25).
Vatican City, BAV, Ross. 502 (Praef. § 17, § 25).
Vatican City, BAV, Barb. Lat. 154 (Praef. § 17, § 25).
Consensus of manuscripts A², R, and B of the α-family (Praef. § 25).
Consensus of manuscripts R and B against A (Praef. § 25).
Lost Roman conjectural recension derived from codex o, heavily contaminated with grammarians' citations and emendations by Lorenzo Valla (ca. mid-15th century) (Praef. §§ 24–26).
Cambridge, University Library, Nn. 2. 40 (saec. XV 3/4, before 1471); oldest extant witness of branch φ (Praef. §§ 24–26).
Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 35.31 (Praef. § 24).
Vatican City, BAV, Vat. Lat. 3275 (extends to VI 561) (Praef. § 24).
Vatican City, BAV, Ottob. Lat. 1136 (Praef. § 24).
Consensus of codices F, C, e, f together with the corrected exemplar o (Praef. § 26).
Codex Neapolitanus, Naples, Biblioteca Nazionale Vittorio Emanuele III, IV E 51, copied and corrected by Pomponio Leto in Rome (1458/1459) (Praef. §§ 26–29).
Correcting hand of Pomponio Leto in codex N, who corrected it in Rome in 1459 with the help of φ (Praef. § 26, § 29).
Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, E 125 sup. (Praef. § 29).
Pietro Odo da Montopoli, humanist corrector of codex s (Praef. § 29).
Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 35.29, with annotations by Angelo Poliziano and others (Praef. § 29).
Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 35.32; second hand (T²) introduces emendations up to I 1038 (Praef. § 29).

projectDesc.p: Prototype of a Digital Scholarly Edition (DSE) of the proem to Book III of Lucretius' De rerum natura, developed for the examination in Digital Scholarly Editing: Theory, Methods, and Practice held by Prof. Paola Italia at the University of Bologna for the academic year 2025/2026, based on the critical text established by Marcus Deufert.

segmentation.p: The critical apparatus is encoded inline using the parallel segmentation method. The <lem> element represents the critical text established by Marcus Deufert (2019), while <rdg> elements record readings from the primary manuscript branches, the indirect tradition, and humanist or modern conjectures.

interpretation.p: The apparatus fontium is kept separate from the critical apparatus and records ancient source attestations (Aug.–saec. IX ex.) as provided by Deufert (Praef. §§ 40–46).
The apparatus ad versus iteratos tracks internal formulaic recurrences across the poem, distinguishing identical repetitions (=) from verbal and thematic similarities (~) (Praef. § 39).

normalization.p: Orthography follows the non-normalized practice of the archetype as preserved in Deufert's text (Praef. §§ 53–55), maintaining archaic spellings, unassimilated prefixes, and the non-distinction between vocalic and consonantal u.

person.note: German classical philologist and professor (born 1970); editor of the 2019 critical edition of Lucretius' De rerum natura.
English classical scholar and critic (1756–1801); editor of an influential edition of Lucretius published in London (1796–1797).
Italian classical philologist and textual critic (1923–2000); renowned scholar of classical reception and Latin textual transmission.
British classical scholar (active early 20th century); author of conjectural emendations to classical Latin poets, including Lucretius (1921).
Greek-Italian Renaissance poet and humanist scholar (ca. 1458–1500); produced major conjectural emendations in his working copy of Lucretius.
Swiss classical scholar and epigraphist (1787–1849); editor of Latin classical texts and philosophical treatises.
German classical and Germanic philologist (1793–1851); established the landmark stemmatic edition and reconstructed the archetype of Lucretius (1850).
English classical scholar and pioneering textual critic (1662–1742); composed marginalia and influential conjectures on the text of Lucretius.
Italian humanist poet and scholar (1429–1503), active in Naples; proposed conjectural emendations to classical Latin poets, including Lucretius.
French classical scholar and philologist (1516–1572); editor of a milestone critical edition and commentary on Lucretius (Paris 1563/1570).
German classical philologist (1867–1929); author of a major critical commentary on Lucretius Book III (1897).
German classical philologist (1894–1973); editor of Fragmenta Poetarum Latinorum and author of textual notes on Lucretius (1930).

British classical scholar (1819–1885), Fellow of Trinity College and first Kennedy Professor of Latin at Cambridge; editor of the fundamental edition, translation and commentary of Lucretius (Cambridge 1864; 3rd ed. 1873, cited as Munro³). At III 82 he posited a lacuna and supplied a verse so as to keep the transmitted suadet at III 84.

Swiss classical philologist (1920–2016), professor at the University of Bern; editor of T. Lucreti Cari De rerum natura libri sex (Zürich 1975), cited as C. Müller. At III 84 he conjectured foede, comparing Lucr. 1, 85.

Italian humanist copyist who in 1507 wrote codex Y of Lucretius (Piacenza, Biblioteca Comunale Passerini-Landi, 33: Placentinus Bibl. comm. Land. 33, a Cippellario a. 1507 exaratus). Cited in Deufert's apparatus at III 84: he was the first to see that the transmitted suadet perverts the syntax of the period (qui primus vidit suadet orationem pervertere) and proposed suauem.

German classical philologist (born 1939), professor at the University of Bonn; textual critic specialised in interpolation in Latin poetry (editor of Seneca's tragedies, Oxford 1986). His Lucretian conjectures are not published in a work of his own: Deufert discussed them with him in person and reports them in M. Deufert, Pseudo-Lukrezisches im Lukrez. Die unechten Verse in Lukrezens “De rerum natura”, Berolini et Novi Eboraci 1996. He once condemned III 85–86 as spurious (Deufert 1996, 52 sq.).

German classical scholar (19th century); editor and commentator of T. Lucreti Cari de rerum natura libri sex. Redigirt und erklärt von Friedrich Bockemüller, Stadis 1874. He anticipated the athetesis of III 85–86.
Early Christian author, rhetorician, and apologist (ca. 250 – ca. 325 AD); preserves indirect quotations from Lucretius in his Divinae Institutiones.
Roman grammarian and lexicographer from Thubursicu (active early 4th century AD); quotes numerous poetic lines in De compendiosa doctrina.
Late Roman provincial author and philosopher (fl. ca. 400 AD); preserves numerous classical poetic citations in his Saturnalia.

Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist and statesman (ca. 4 BC – AD 65); quotes Lucretius' simile of the children frightened in the dark (III 87–88 = II 55–56) in his Epistulae morales ad Lucilium (110, 6), reading ita instead of sic.

argument.p: Traditio textus (vv. 1–621): Ω (= O Γ [= Q V]). The text of this section rests upon the consensus of the Carolingian archetype Ω, witnessed by O and the Γ-branch (Q and V). Critical text follows Deufert (2019).

div.head: Apparatus fontium (III 1–93)
div.note:
Cf. Lactantius inst. 6, 2, 6: lumen …, ut ait poeta, ‘liquidum’ atque ‘clarum’.
In Divinae institutiones (6, 2, 6), Lactantius writes: «Aliud vero ille a nobis exigit lumen, et quidem non fumidum, sed (ut ait poeta) liquidum atque clarum», explicitly quoting the noun lumen and the adjective clarum, while also pairing them with liquidum.

div.head: Apparatus versuum iteratorum
div.note: tremulis facere artubus haedi (III.7) echoes a similar internal parallel at II.367 (tremulis cum uocibus haedi), where the image of newborn goats is likewise characterized by trembling.

Et quoniam docui cunctarum exordia rerum / qualia sint et quam uariis distantia formis / sponte sua uolitent aeterno percita motu / quoue modo possint res ex his quaeque creari (III.31–34) is repeated verbatim at IV.45–48, serving as a formulaic didactic recapitulation of the atomic principles established in the first two books.

Et quoniam docui (III.31) recurs identically at VI.43 and with slight structural variations at I.951, II.478, II.522 and IV.45, operating as one of Lucretius' standard transitions to link a completed argument to a new topic.
qualia sint et quam uariis distantia formis (III.32) closely mirrors II.334 (qualia sint et quam longe distantia formis) to reintroduce the treatment of atomic shapes.
uolitent aeterno percita motu (III.33) repeats verbatim the clausula at II.1055, deploying the same fixed formula to describe the incessant, unguided trajectory of atoms through the void.

sed magis in primis animum (III.45) repeats the verse opening verbatim at III.181, deploying the same emphatic transitional formula to direct the reader's immediate attention to the nature of the mind (animus).

noctes atque dies niti praestante labore / ad summas emergere opes (III.62–63) repeats verbatim the programmatic distich at II.12–13, deploying the same formulaic critique of blind human ambition and the exhausting struggle for political and material supremacy.

nam ueluti pueri trepidant atque omnia caecis / in tenebris metuunt, sic nos in luce timemus (III.87–88): cf. ad II.55–56 (see also VI.35–36). The simile of the children frightened in the dark recurs verbatim from Book II; the indirect tradition (Seneca, Epist. 110, 6, reading ita for sic) is recorded there.

nam ueluti pueri trepidant … sed naturae species ratioque (III.87–93) is repeated verbatim at II.55–61 and VI.35–41: a seven-line formulaic block sealing the proems of Books II, III and VI, stating that only reason, not wealth, power or sunlight, dispels human fears.

hunc igitur terrorem animi tenebrasque necessest / non radii solis neque lucida tela diei / discutiant, sed naturae species ratioque (III.91–93) repeats verbatim I.146–148, where the tercet first states the programme of the poem: only the observation of nature and reason (naturae species ratioque) free the mind from terror.
non radii solis neque lucida tela diei (III.92): cf. ad I.147 (see also II.60 and VI.40), where the image of the sun's rays as shining darts first appears and its parallels are recorded.

lg.l: In the murk of our darkness, you, Epicurus, raised your blazing lantern
to show us the blessings of life.
And I follow you,
walking with confident footsteps the trails that you have blazed,
not to be your rival, but in admiration and love,
and happy to have your example to guide me. How could I think of competing with you? A swallow might as well vie
with swans, or a young kid on its wobbly legs presume to race
alongside a strong horse.
You are our father, our leader, our pioneer, discovering truths that you share with us.
You are our guide, and from your writings,
You are like one of those bees that goes out to find the flowers and then brings back word to the hive of where the sweet nectar is for them all.
So do we feed on your words
of perdurable gold that are worthy of everlasting life.
We begin to follow your thoughts, your arguments, and your reasons,
about the nature of things, sprung from a divine mind,
and our mind’s terrors abate, while the opaque walls of the world
open wide to exhibit the intricate actions and movements that go on all the time throughout the limitless void.
Through you, I see the gods in their tranquil dwelling places,
where no harsh winds ever blow, where no dark clouds approach with the threat of violent storms,
and it never snows or freezes,
but a gentle air surrounds them attendant on their pleasures,
and smiles in an expanse of bounteous light.
nature never obtrudes on their lofty peace of mind
but amplifies their delight.
To them, Acheron’s gloomy regions are an unlikely story.
They look down on the earth beneath
and watch with the same keen understanding as you, Epicurus, have taught to us,
the intricateness of nature’s inner workings
that I contemplate with awe and an all but divine delight
in what you expound and explain.
I have already described the atoms, the seeds of things,
their different shapes
and motions as they fly about on their own,
and how all things in the world are derived from their combinations.
The next subject to which we turn our attention is the mind, the animus,
and the spirit, the anima,
and the way to get rid of the fear of death that troubles us all,
tainting all our delights
and shadowing every moment with Acheron’s gloom.
[leaving no joy pure and unalloyed.]
More than they fear the pains of disease
or guilt and shame, men dread the bottomless chasm of death.
Some there are who claim that the soul, which is in the blood,
or perhaps in the air we breathe, survives and never dies,
and they have no use for logic and reason.
But I shall explain
their ideas are fantastic and their hopes not based upon fact.
Take some poor fellow,
banished for his disgraceful crime,
living beyond the edge of nowhere, but still alive.
What does he do but continue his sacrifices
of cattle and prayers to his forebears’ ghosts,
and, in his misery,
hope for a less wretched life than this in another and better world?
It is always in such adversity that we learn what a man is made of,
what truth or what superstition informs his thoughts and actions,
and what resources he brings with which to confront his troubles.
The mask is torn away, and you look at his real face.
Bizarrely enough it is that fear of death that ruins the life of a man
as he strives for wealth and power, scheming and plotting,
forcing miserable mortals to transgress all bounds of law
day and night to climb the greasy pole by fair means or foul,
striving to emerge into the heights of sovereign power.
These wounds of life are nourished in no small part by the dread of death.
Even though he’s afraid of men’s scorn and grinding poverty,
his real worry is that he may wake up one day far removed from a sweet and stable life,
lingering already, as it were, before the very gates of death;
and from this, driven by baseless panic, he strives to escape,
wishing to banish the specter far, far away from himself.
The sweetness of life and its simple pleasures he overlooks,
as he vies with other men, amassing wealth, greedy, adding slaughter to slaughter,
ruthless even to doing murder, rejoicing in the death of a brother,
and fearing and loathing the banquet tables of his own kinsmen.
For like reason he never ventures to dine without terror,
fearing his wine goblet may be poisoned as well.
In the same way he is consumed with bitter envy
of someone with pomp and power who parades through the town in glory,
while he himself wallows in obscurity’s murky shadows.
Men wear themselves out and perish for the sake of statues
and an enduring name proclaimed on the marble plinth.
The fear of death corrupts the love of life and the light,
breeding self-hatred and driving men to suicide,
forgetting that this very terror is the fountain of all their cares,
the poison that shatters modesty and breaks the bonds of friendship,
overturning piety from its deepest foundations.
For their fear of death some men dishonor themselves and betray
their friends, even their dear parents and fatherland,
all in the desperate hope of postponing that journey to Acheron’s bleak kingdom.
Just as children in blind darkness tremble and imagine terrible monsters,
so do we, in the light of day, fear things that are no more frightful
than what children dread in the night, imagining ghastly horrors of decease.
This dread in the mind’s dark recess neither the rays of the sun
nor daylight can dispel, but only reason and the contemplation of nature’s laws.

div.head: Index of Philosophical Keywords (lines 1–93)
div.p: Key concepts of Epicurean doctrine and Lucretian poetic imagery appearing in the proem to Book III.

sense.def: Light of Epicurean truth and scientific enlightenment. It opens the proem (line 1) in stark contrast to the darkness of human ignorance, and concludes the Olympian vision of the gods (line 22) radiant in an expanse of bounteous brightness.
Rational explanation and philosophical system of Epicurus. It loudly proclaims (vociferari) the physical nature of things, dispelling unfounded superstitious terrors through logical inquiry.
The void: one of the two foundational principles of Epicurean atomism alongside solid bodies. An intangible, infinite space through which matter moves, combines, and dissolves unceasingly.
The walls of the world: the visible boundaries of the cosmic sphere. Upon the revelation of Epicurean physics, these restrictive ramparts withdraw and fall away, opening the mind to infinite space.

Darkness, the counter-image of the Epicurean lumen: the social obscurity of the envious (line 77), the dark in which children fear imaginary dangers (lines 88, 90), and finally the darkness of the mind (tenebras animi) that only reason can dispel (line 91).

Dutiful devotion towards gods, family and fatherland, the core of Roman morality. The fear of death overturns it from its foundations (line 84), driving men to betray their country and their parents (lines 85–86).

The outward aspect and rational observation of nature. Joined with ratio in the programmatic formula naturae species ratioque (line 93 = I 148), it is the only remedy that can dispel the terrors and darkness of the mind.

The gloomy regions of the underworld, named after the river Acheron. They vanish once the structure of the universe is understood (line 25), yet the fear of them drives men to betray fatherland and parents (line 86).
Pleasure, the supreme ethical good of Epicurean doctrine: the divine delight of contemplating nature (line 28), which the fear of death prevents from remaining pure and unalloyed (line 40).
The fear of death and of punishment after death, root of human anxiety and moral degradation, which must be driven out by physical doctrine (line 37); it returns as mortis formido (lines 64, 79).
The two components of the soul in Epicurean psychology: the rational mind (animus), seated in the breast, and the vital spirit (anima), spread through the whole body; both are corporeal and mortal.
Superstitious fear and ritual obsession born of ignorance of natural causes; adversity reveals its hold on those who boast of philosophical self-sufficiency (line 54).
